point: The review covers hydraulic modelling, stochasticity, market participation and solution methods, comparing the literature and linking it to this project.
Literature was found through keyword searches in several databases and an AI retrieval tool, filtered by quality-check questions.
Selected papers had to meet the quality questions, and further papers were found by backward snowballing from their references.
Adding stochasticity improves profit, reduces spillage risk and gives more robust strategies than deterministic models, as a case study showed.
Inflow is a recognised key uncertainty, and temperature can be stochastic too because it drives inflow and demand-based prices.
Studies model stochastic prices in different configurations, though stochastic prices in every market would cause dimensionality problems.
The literature converges on including stochasticity for realism, with prices and inflows the most prominent stochastic variables.
Price uncertainty matters most for price takers, inflow uncertainty matters regardless, and researchers limit stochastic variables for tractability.
Accurate hydraulic modelling is often essential, and choosing a production function method trades computational complexity against model detail.
Production function methods such as piecewise linearisation and MILP vary with the model purpose, and MILP becomes heavy as problems grow.
A mid-term model avoids variable head by correcting efficiency with head sensitivities from separate simulations, a lighter alternative to MILP.
Successive linear programming updates head-dependent efficiency iteratively, and head optimisation improves the solution especially for half-full reservoirs.
Hydraulic modelling can decide model performance but raises complexity, so the level of detail should fit the model purpose.
Hydropower operates across several markets, so modelling them gives more realistic value estimates than single-market models.
Coordinated bidding in day-ahead and reserve markets yields clear gains, though assuming a fixed activation share may overstate results.
Ignoring reserve activation systematically underestimates costs, which for producers means lost water value, changed reservoir management and extra unit wear.
A day-ahead and intraday co-optimisation model with block and hourly bids runs on a rolling horizon from a price-taker view.
Intraday participation added negligible profit in this study, unlike the day-ahead and reserve case, though studies are not directly comparable.
One study covers many markets but is multi-objective with emissions, and omits added value discussion and balancing direction.
Forward contracts for a price-making hydro and pumped storage plant raised profit by a fifth, though under assumptions of known contract prices.
The added value of a joint formulation across all eligible markets is largely absent from the literature, and omitting activation may understate costs.
The method chosen shapes how flexibility, uncertainty and value are represented, so solution methods are reviewed to position the work.
SDP and SDDP are used at all horizons, decomposing a year into weekly problems with forward and backward passes.
Another SDP study uses daily mixed-integer subproblems, and SDDP may beat SDP computationally because its cost grows linearly with scenarios.
Benders decomposition, related to SDP and SDDP, suits long-term hydro-thermal planning and gave better hydro utilisation than a standard long-term model.
Benders decomposition splits a large energy system MILP into an investment master and weekly operational subproblems solved in parallel.
Benders decomposition also handles short-term scheduling with full AC power flow, so it is relevant at any horizon.
Scenario-tree stochastic programming loses effective uncertainty deeper in the tree and scales poorly, so successive linear programming suits only short-term problems.
Multi-objective optimisation traces a profit and emissions trade-off, which lies outside this project's scope but is a future direction.
Method choice depends on stochasticity, non-linearity, stages, horizon and objectives, with SDDP most promising when all are considered.
A table compares the reviewed literature across the four dimensions and shows this report's contribution.
No study jointly covers day-ahead, intraday, FCR and aFRR markets without modelling activation, which is the identified research gap.
The gap suggests modelling fuller market participation and its effects on water values and revenues from a capacity expansion view.
The model includes hydraulic behaviour and stays deterministic, while stochastic extensions and solution methods are outlined in the review.
